verses.zh: 巴比伦王伯沙撒元年，但以理在床上做梦，见了脑中的异象，就记录这梦，述说其中的大意。
verses.en: In the first[NOTE:1] year of King Belshazzar of Babylon, Daniel had[NOTE:2] a dream filled with visions[NOTE:3] while he was lying on his bed. Then he wrote down the dream in summary fashion.[NOTE:4]
notes: The first year of Belshazzar’s reign would have been ca. 553 b.c. Daniel would have been approximately 67 years old at the time of this vision.
Aram “saw.”

Aram “and visions of his head.” The Aramaic is difficult here. Some scholars add a verb thought to be missing (e.g., “the visions of his head [were alarming him]”), but there is no external evidence to support such a decision, and the awkwardness of the text at this point may be original.
Aram “head of words.” The phrase is absent in Theodotion. Cf. NIV’s “the substance of his dream.”

verses.zh: 但以理说：我夜里见异象，看见天的四风陡起，刮在大海之上。
verses.en: Daniel explained:[NOTE:1] “I was watching in my vision during the night as[NOTE:2] the four winds of the sky[NOTE:3] were stirring up the great sea.[NOTE:4]
notes: Aram “answered and said.”
Aram “and behold.”
Or “the heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.
The referent of the great sea is unclear. The common view that the expression refers to the Mediterranean Sea is conjectural.

verses.zh: 有四个大兽从海中上来，形状各有不同：
verses.en: Then four large beasts came up from the sea; they were different from one another.

verses.zh: 头一个像狮子，有鹰的翅膀；我正观看的时候，兽的翅膀被拔去，兽从地上得立起来，用两脚站立，像人一样，又得了人心。
verses.en: “The first one was like a lion with eagles’ wings. As I watched, its wings were pulled off, and it was lifted up from the ground. It was made to stand on two feet like a human being, and a human mind[NOTE:1] was given to it.[NOTE:2]
notes: Aram “heart of a man.”

The identity of the first animal, derived from v. 17 and the parallels in chap. 2, is Babylon. The reference to the plucking of its wings is probably a reference to the time of Nebuchadnezzar’s insanity (cf. chap. 4). The latter part of v. 4 then describes the restoration of Nebuchadnezzar. The other animals have traditionally been understood to represent respectively Media-Persia, Greece, and Rome, although most of modern scholarship identifies them as Media, Persia, and Greece. For a biblical parallel to the mention of lion, bear, and leopard together, see Hos 13:7-8.

verses.zh: 又有一兽如熊，就是第二兽，旁跨而坐，口齿内衔着三根肋骨。有吩咐这兽的说：起来吞吃多肉。
verses.en: “Then[NOTE:1] a second beast appeared, like a bear. It was raised up on one side, and there were three ribs[NOTE:2] in its mouth between its teeth.[NOTE:3] It was told,[NOTE:4] ‘Get up and devour much flesh!’
notes: Aram “and behold.”

The three ribs held securely in the mouth of the bear, perhaps representing Media-Persia, apparently symbolize military conquest, but the exact identity of the “ribs” is not clear. Possibly it is a reference to the Persian conquest of Lydia, Egypt, and Babylonia.
The LXX lacks the phrase “between its teeth.”
Aram “and thus they were saying to it.”

verses.zh: 此后我观看，又有一兽如豹，背上有鸟的四个翅膀；这兽有四个头，又得了权柄。
verses.en: “After these things,[NOTE:1] as I was watching, another beast[NOTE:2] like a leopard appeared, with four bird-like wings on its back.[NOTE:3] This beast had four heads,[NOTE:4] and ruling authority was given to it.
notes: Aram “this,” as also in v. 7.
Aram “and behold, another one.”
Or “sides.”
If the third animal is Greece, the most likely identification of these four heads is the fourfold division of the empire of Alexander the Great following his death (see note on Dan 8:8).

verses.zh: 其后我在夜间的异象中观看，见第四兽甚是可怕，极其强壮，大有力量，有大铁牙，吞吃嚼碎，所剩下的用脚践踏。这兽与前三兽大不相同，头有十角。
verses.en: “After these things, as I was watching in the night visions[NOTE:1] a fourth beast appeared—one dreadful, terrible, and very strong.[NOTE:2] It had two large rows[NOTE:3] of iron teeth. It devoured and crushed, and anything that was left it trampled with its feet. It was different from all the beasts that came before it, and it had 10 horns.
notes: The Aramaic text has also “and behold,” as also in vv. 8, 13.

The fourth animal differs from the others in that it is nondescript. Apparently it was so fearsome that Daniel could find nothing with which to compare it. Attempts to identify this animal as an elephant or other known creature are conjectural.
The Aramaic word for “teeth” is dual rather than plural, suggesting two rows of teeth.

verses.zh: 我正观看这些角，见其中又长起一个小角；先前的角中有三角在这角前，连根被它拔出来。这角有眼，像人的眼，有口说夸大的话。
verses.en: “As I was contemplating the horns, another horn—a small one—came up between them, and three of the former horns were torn out by the roots to make room for it.[NOTE:1] This horn had eyes resembling human eyes and a mouth speaking arrogant[NOTE:2] things.
notes: Aram “were uprooted from before it.”
Aram “great,” as also in vv. 11, 20.

verses.zh: 我观看，见有宝座设立，上头坐着亘古常在者。他的衣服洁白如雪，头发如纯净的羊毛。宝座乃火焰，其轮乃烈火。
verses.en: “While I was watching,thrones were set up,and the Ancient of Days[NOTE:1] took his seat.His attire was white like snow;the hair of his head was like lamb’s[NOTE:2] wool.His throne was ablaze with fire,and its wheels were all aflame.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “the Ancient One” (NAB, NRSV, NLT), although the traditional expression has been retained in the present translation because it is familiar to many readers (cf. TEV “One who had been living for ever”; CEV “the Eternal God”).

Traditionally the Aramaic word נְקֵא (neqeʾ) has been rendered “pure,” but here it more likely means “of a lamb.” Cf. the Syriac neqyaʾ (“a sheep, ewe”). On this word, see further, M. Sokoloff, “ʾamar neqeʾ, ‘Lamb’s Wool’ (Dan 7:9),” JBL 95 (1976): 277-79.
Aram “a flaming fire.”

verses.zh: 从他面前有火，像河发出；事奉他的有千千，在他面前侍立的有万万；他坐着要行审判，案卷都展开了。
verses.en: A river of fire was streaming forthand proceeding from his presence.Many thousands were ministering to him;many tens of thousands stood ready to serve him.[NOTE:1] The court convened,[NOTE:2] and the books were opened.
notes: Aram “were standing before him.”
Aram “judgment sat.”

verses.zh: 那时我观看，见那兽因小角说夸大话的声音被杀，身体损坏，扔在火中焚烧。
verses.en: “Then I kept on watching because of the arrogant words of the horn that was speaking. I was watching[NOTE:1] until the beast was killed and its body destroyed and thrown into[NOTE:2] the flaming fire.
notes: The LXX and Theodotion lack the words “I was watching” here. It is possible that these words in the MT are a dittography from the first part of the verse.
Aram “and given over to” (so NRSV).

verses.zh: 其余的兽，权柄都被夺去，生命却仍存留，直到所定的时候和日期。
verses.en: As for the rest of the beasts, their ruling authority had already been removed, though they were permitted to go on living[NOTE:1] for a time and a season.
notes: Aram “a prolonging of life was granted to them.”

verses.zh: 我在夜间的异象中观看，见有一位像人子的，驾着天云而来，被领到亘古常在者面前，
verses.en: “I was watching in the night visions,and with[NOTE:1] the clouds of the sky,[NOTE:2] one like a son of man[NOTE:3] was approaching.He went up to the Ancient of Daysand was escorted[NOTE:4] before him.
notes: The LXX has ἐπί (epi, “upon”) here (cf. Matt 24:30; 26:64). Theodotion has μετά (meta, “with”) here (cf. Mark 14:62; Rev 1:7).
Or “the heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heavens” or “sky” depending on the context.

This text is probably the main OT background for Jesus’ use of the term “son of man.” In both Jewish and Christian circles the reference in the book of Daniel has traditionally been understood to refer to an individual, usually in a messianic sense. Many modern scholars, however, understand the reference to have a corporate identity. In this view, the “son of man” is to be equated with the “holy ones” (vv. 18, 21, 22, 25) or the “people of the holy ones” (v. 27) and understood as a reference to the Jewish people. Others understand Daniel’s reference to be to the angel Michael.
Aram “they brought him near.”

verses.zh: 得了权柄、荣耀、国度，使各方、各国、各族的人都事奉他。他的权柄是永远的，不能废去；他的国必不败坏。
verses.en: To him was given ruling authority, honor, and sovereignty.All peoples, nations, and language groups were serving[NOTE:1] him.His authority is eternal and will not pass away.[NOTE:2] His kingdom will not be destroyed.[NOTE:3]
notes: Some take “serving” here in the sense of “worshiping.”
Aram “is an eternal authority that will not pass away.”
Aram “is one that will not be destroyed.”

verses.zh: 至于我―但以理，我的灵在我里面愁烦，我脑中的异象使我惊惶。
verses.en: “As for me, Daniel, my spirit was distressed,[NOTE:1] and the visions of my mind[NOTE:2] were alarming me.
notes: The Aramaic text includes the phrase “in its sheath,” apparently viewing the body as a container or receptacle for the spirit somewhat like a sheath or scabbard is for a knife or a sword (cf. NAB “within its sheath of flesh”). For this phrase the LXX and Vulgate have “in these things.”
Aram “head.”

verses.zh: 我就近一位侍立者，问他这一切的真情。他就告诉我，将那事的讲解给我说明。
verses.en: I approached one of those standing nearby and asked him about the meaning[NOTE:1] of all this. So he spoke with me and revealed[NOTE:2] to me the interpretation of the vision:[NOTE:3]
notes: Aram “what is certain.”
Aram “and made known.”
Aram “matter,” but the matter at hand is of course the vision.

verses.zh: 这四个大兽就是四王将要在世上兴起。
verses.en: ‘These large beasts, which are four in number, represent four kings who will arise from the earth.

verses.zh: 然而，至高者的圣民，必要得国享受，直到永永远远。
verses.en: The holy ones[NOTE:1] of the Most High will receive the kingdom and will take possession of the kingdom forever and ever.’
notes: The expression holy ones is either a reference to angels, to human beings devoted to God, or to both. The context is an earthly kingdom the holy ones will possess, and man was appointed to rule the earth (Gen 1:28). The holy ones are defeated and harassed by an earthly ruler in 7:21, 25, and human rulers cannot defeat and harass angels. So the holy ones are almost certainly human beings devoted to God.

verses.zh: 那时我愿知道第四兽的真情，它为何与那三兽的真情大不相同，甚是可怕，有铁牙铜爪，吞吃嚼碎，所剩下的用脚践踏；
verses.en: “Then I wanted to know the meaning[NOTE:1] of the fourth beast, which was different from all the others. It was very dreadful, with two rows of iron teeth and bronze claws, and it devoured, crushed, and trampled anything that was left with its feet.
notes: Aram “to make certain.”

verses.zh: 头有十角和那另长的一角，在这角前有三角被它打落。这角有眼，有说夸大话的口，形状强横，过于它的同类。
verses.en: I also wanted to know[NOTE:1] the meaning of the 10 horns on its head, and of that other horn that came up and before which three others fell. This was the horn that had eyes[NOTE:2] and a mouth speaking arrogant things, whose appearance was more formidable than the others.[NOTE:3]
notes: The words “I also wanted to know” are added in the translation for stylistic reasons.
The conjunction in the MT before “eyes” is odd. The ancient versions do not seem to presuppose it.
Aram “greater than its companions.”

verses.zh: 我观看，见这角与圣民争战，胜了他们。
verses.en: While I was watching, that horn began to wage war against the holy ones and was defeating[NOTE:1] them,
notes: Aram “prevailing against” (KJV, ASV both similar); NASB “overpowering them”; TEV “conquered them.”

verses.zh: 直到亘古常在者来给至高者的圣民伸冤，圣民得国的时候就到了。
verses.en: until the Ancient of Days arrived and judgment was rendered[NOTE:1] in favor of the holy ones of the Most High. Then the time came for the holy ones to take possession of the kingdom.
notes: In the LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate the verb is active, understanding “judgment” to be the object rather than the subject of the verb (i.e., “the Ancient of Days rendered judgment”). This presupposes a different vocalization of the verb ( יְהַב [yehav] rather than the MT יְהִב [yehiv]).

verses.zh: 那侍立者这样说：第四兽就是世上必有的第四国，与一切国大不相同，必吞吃全地，并且践踏嚼碎。
verses.en: “This is what he told me:[NOTE:1] ‘The fourth beast means that there will be a fourth kingdom on earththat will differ from all the other kingdoms.It will devour all the earthand will trample and crush it.
notes: Aram “thus he said.”

verses.zh: 至于那十角，就是从这国中必兴起的十王，后来又兴起一王，与先前的不同；他必制伏三王。
verses.en: The 10 horns mean that 10 kings will arise from that kingdom.Another king will arise after them,but he will be different from the earlier ones.He will humiliate[NOTE:1] three kings.
notes: Or “subjugate”; KJV, NASB, NIV “subdue”; ASV, NRSV “put down.”

verses.zh: 他必向至高者说夸大的话，必折磨至高者的圣民，必想改变节期和律法。圣民必交付他手一载、二载、半载。
verses.en: He will speak words against the Most High.He will harass[NOTE:1] the holy ones of the Most High continually.His intention will be[NOTE:2] to change times established by law.[NOTE:3] The holy ones will be delivered into his handfor a time, times,[NOTE:4] and half a time.
notes: Aram “wear out” (so KJV, ASV, NRSV); NASB, NLT “wear down.” The word is a hapax legomenon in biblical Aramaic, but in biblical Hebrew it especially refers to wearing out such things as garments. Here it is translated “harass…continually.”
Aram “he will think.”
Aram “times and law.” The present translation is based on the understanding that the expression is a hendiadys.

Although the word times is vocalized in the MT as a plural, it probably should be regarded as a dual. The Masoretes may have been influenced here by the fact that in late Aramaic (and Syriac) the dual forms fall out of use. The meaning would thus be three and a half “times.”

verses.zh: 然而，审判者必坐着行审判；他的权柄必被夺去，毁坏，灭绝，一直到底。
verses.en: But the court will convene,[NOTE:1] and his ruling authority will be removed—destroyed and abolished forever!
notes: Aram “judgment will sit” (KJV similar).

verses.zh: 国度、权柄，和天下诸国的大权必赐给至高者的圣民。他的国是永远的；一切掌权的都必事奉他，顺从他。
verses.en: Then the kingdom, authority,and greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heavenwill be delivered to the people of the holy ones[NOTE:1] of the Most High.His kingdom is an eternal kingdom; all authorities will serve him and obey him.’
notes: If the “holy ones” are angels, then this probably refers to the angels as protectors of God’s people. If the “holy ones” are God’s people, then this is an appositional construction, “the people who are the holy ones.” See 8:24 for the corresponding Hebrew phrase and the note there.

verses.zh: 那事至此完毕。至于我―但以理，心中甚是惊惶，脸色也改变了，却将那事存记在心。
verses.en: “This is the conclusion of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts troubled me greatly, and the color drained from my face.[NOTE:1] But I kept the matter to myself.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Aram “my brightness was changing on me.”
Aram “in my heart.”

Many scholars want the order to be Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece. This is usually because
they identify the blasphemous Little Horn to be Antiochus Epiphanes IV, who the Jews named Epimames ("the mad"), But,
Media was never a separate world empire. It is always linked to and subservient to Persia.

- The kingdoms seem to be:

- Neo-Babylonian (Dan. 2:37-38, Nebuchadnezzar II)

- Medo-Persia (Dan. 8:20, Cyrus II, the Great)

- Greece (Dan. 8:21, Alexander the Great)

- Rome

- the Eternal Kingdom of God (Dan. 2:45, Messianic, Son of Man, Dan. 7:13)

- These Gentile kingdoms became progressively anti-God. It is surprising that these kingdoms, which seem to be in
chronological order (cf. Dan. 7:17, are crushed simultaneously (cf. Dan. 2:35,45). This crushing represents God's ultimate
and complete victory (cf. Dan. 2:44; 7:14,18,27), not that all these empires have to be in power or in existence at the
same time (cf. Dan. 7:11-12).

God's complete control and sovereignty of all historical events, both individual and national is the theological
theme of the book of Daniel (i.e., Dan. 2:21; 4:17,32).

- This chapter continues the Aramaic section, which unites the two obvious literary divisions (chapters 1-6 and 7-12) of Daniel. Chapters 2-7
are addressed to Gentile rulers and deal with Gentile nations so they are addressed in Aramaic. The remaining chapters are addressed
specifically to God's people and are in Hebrew.

- This begins the visions of Daniel which overlap the events of Daniel 1-6. These visions have an affinity in genre to both Hebrew
prophecy and apocalyptic literature (which began in Isaiah, but is fully developed in Daniel 7-12 and Zechariah).

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

- The poetic sections of this chapter (Dan.7:9-10; 13-14) are the theological heart of the book. They capsule God's eternal purpose
and plan for human redemption-the Messiah! They speak of victory through suffering for the saints of the Highest One
(cf. Dan. 7:21-22,25,27).

This text (especially Dan. 7:13-14) is the origin of Jesus' use of the phrase "Son of Man," which reveals His true humanity and
divinity (cf. John 1:1-14; Phil. 2:6-11; Col. 1:15-18; Heb. 1:1-3;1 John 4:1-3).

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: DANIEL 7:1-8

1In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon Daniel saw a dream and
visions in his mind as he lay on his bed; then he wrote the dream down and related the following summary of it. 2Daniel
said, "I was looking in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea. 3And four great beasts
were coming up from the sea, different from one another. 4The first was like a lion and had the wings of an eagle. I kept
looking until its wings were plucked, and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man; a human mind also was given to it.
5And behold, another beast, a second one, resembling a bear. And it was raised up on one side, and three ribs were in its mouth
between its teeth; and thus they said to it, ‘Arise, devour much meat!' 6After this I kept looking, and behold, another one, like a
leopard, which had on its back four wings of a bird; the beast also had four heads, and dominion was given to it. 7After this I kept looking
in the night visions, and behold, a fourth beast, dreadful and terrifying and extremely strong; and it had large iron teeth. It devoured and crushed and
trampled down the remainder with its feet; and it was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns. 8While I was
contemplating the horns, behold, another horn, a little one, came up among them, and three of the first horns were pulled out by the roots before it; and
behold, this horn possessed eyes like the eyes of a man and a mouth uttering great boasts."

7:1 "In the first year of Belshazzar" This shows that the book is not written in chronological order
(cf. Daniel 5, which is the fall of the city of Babylon with Belshazzar in charge in October of 539 B.C.). The date
mentioned in the text would be about 552-551 B.C., which is fourteen years before chapter 5. This was
when Belshazzar's father, King Nabonidus, moved his official residence to Teima in Arabia. It is uncertain exactly when Belshazzar became
co-regent, but 552 B.C. is a good guess.

The Aramaic section of Daniel goes from Dan. 2:4 through 7:28, which marks it as a literary unit. Therefore,
we must relate chapter 7 with what goes before, as well as with what follows.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NE0-BABYLON

▣ "Daniel saw" It is interesting that chapters 1-6 are written in the third person, as is
Dan. 7:1, but the first person predominates chapters 7-12 (e.g., Dan. 7:2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11[twice], 13, 15,
16, 19, 21, 28).

▣ "a dream and visions" In chapters 1-6 the divine dreams were given to Gentile rulers, which is rare
in the OT (cf. Pharaoh and Joseph), but in chapters 7-12 the revelations from YHWH come to Daniel personally.

The apparent distinction between dreams and visions is not the level of inspiration, but
whether one is asleep or awake, unconscious or conscious. In this context Daniel is obviously in bed, but
it is unspecified if he was asleep. In this context the two terms are synonyms of God's special revelations
to Daniel about how these Gentile empires will affect the people of God.

p. 141, who says this is possible, but not likely).

From Daniel's style of writing the two phrases in Dan. 7:1b ("wrote" and "related") are
parallel with no distinction. Notice the next verse, "answered and said," typifies the repetitive style
of Daniel.

7:2 "the four winds of heaven" Four is the biblical symbolic number for the world (i.e., the four
corners of the earth, cf. Dan. 8:8; 11:4; Zech. 2:6; 6:5; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #2). This has been interpreted as

- universal divine knowledge (cf. Zech. 1:8-11; 6:1-8)

- a gathering of angels (cf. Isa. 11:12; Matt. 13:41; 24:31; Mark 13:27)

- destroying angels (cf. Jer. 49:36; Zech. 2:6; Rev. 7:1; 9:14-15)

This and similar phrases are imagery for God's activity in the world (where "four" is
combined with "winds," "corners," "angels"). God knows and allows/controls all activity on planet earth
(i.e., Dan. 2:21; 4:17,32).

"Heaven" refers to the atmosphere of this planet.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

▣ "were stirring up" God was active in sending the "four winds of heaven" to disrupt earthly
activities. This chapter is yet another emphasis on God's sovereign control of history and the nations (i.e., all humanity).

7:2-3 "the great sea. . .the sea" There have been several theories of the meaning of this phrase:

- it refers literally to the Mediterranean Ocean (cf. Num. 34:6, 7; Joshua 9:1)

- it is imagery for all the nations of the earth (cf. Dan. 7:17; Ps. 65:7; Isa. 17:12-13; 57:20; Rev. 17:15)

- it refers to the initial watery chaos which was part of creation (cf. Gen. 1:2; 7:11; 49:25; Ps. 36:6; Isa. 51:10; Amos 7:4;
see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WATERS and also IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 740)

As always context determines meaning. Here it refers to the known world of the Ancient Near
East, that part of the world which affects the people of God and the Promised Land.

▣ Just an added note about "the sea." It seems theologically significant. It is used regularly in ANE
mythology related to creation (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: CREATION AND FLOOD ACCOUNTS IN THE ANE).

In the Bible the imagery, after the fall of mankind in Genesis 3, is directed toward a way of referring to
"rebellious" mankind. This fits this text and the one in the book of Revelation where it mentions

- a beast that comes out of the sea, Rev. 13:1 (similar to Daniel)

- a sea of glass before the throne in heaven, Rev. 4:6, which symbolizes the holiness of God

- sinners cannot approach

- the saved can, Rev. 15:2

- one day the sea that "separates" will be removed, Rev. 21:18

See exegetical notes at Rev. 4:6 and 21:1 online.

7:3 "And four great beasts were coming up from the sea, different from one another" This seems to
imply simultaneous kingdoms (cf. Dan. 7:12 and 2:44), but the extended contexts of chapters 2 and 8 demand
sequential kingdoms.

There are several aspects to this description that would have intensified a negative Jewish
reaction to this vision.

- The great surging ocean would have been fearful to those accustomed to the semi-arid life of
Palestine. Jews never were extensively involved in maritime trade. Even Solomon's fleet was manned
by foreigners (Phoenicians).

- Predatory, Levitically unclean animals were attacking humanity.

- Animals of composite types would violate the "after their kind" of Genesis 1 and Leviticus laws.

- The inhumanity of these pagan empires (especially the fourth empire, cf. Dan. 7:7,23).

- The blasphemy of the little horn against God (cf. Dan. 7:8,11,20,25).

7:4 "The first was like a lion" Notice the word "like" used here is from an Aramaic
PREPOSITION. This same idea is repeated in Dan. 7:5, but with the Aramaic word demah
(cf. Dan. 3:25). In Dan. 7:6 the PREPOSITION is used again. The whole point is that what
Daniel saw was not real earthly animals, but similar to known animals with different physical attributes
(i.e., winged lion, winged leopard). These are apocalyptic symbols of rulers and empires.

▣ "which had the wings of an eagle" The Babylonian army is described as a swooping
eagle (cf. Jer. 49:22; Ezek. 17:3; Hab. 1:8). This was imagery to describe the speed of their advance.

▣ "its wings were plucked" This is imagery for a military defeat. These powerful, national
armies seemed invincible, but in reality they were still just human armies.

Notice how often in this verse divine action is directed toward the Gentile empire:

- "wings were plucked" (BDB 1101, Piel PERFECT)

- "it was lifted up" (BDB 1102, Piel PERFECT)

- "made to stand" (BDB 1110, Hoph PERFECT)

- "human mind also was given to it" (Piel PRESENT) [this is true of "was raised up
on one side," Dan. 7:5]

God is in complete control (cf. Dan. 2:21). Some commentators believe that these actions reflect
Nebuchadnezzar's madness in chapter 4. Although this is possible, again interpreters must be careful of
trying to find a historical referent to all the details of Daniel's visions.

▣ "made to stand on two feet like a man; a human mind also was given to it" Some commentators
think this refers to

- Nebuchadnezzar's madness and restoration of chapter 4

- the barbaric Chaldeans becoming more civilized and cultured after their initial conquest
(i.e., affected by Sumerian culture)

However, the phrase is very ambiguous and may simply be an apocalyptic detail which was
never meant to have a historical fulfillment. This powerful empire existed and was destroyed, making room
for the next empire from the Ancient Near East.

7:5 "a bear" This is another powerful predator of the Near East, which is used often in the OT
paralleled with lion (cf. 1 Sam. 17:34,36,37; Prov. 28:15; Amos 5:19; Rev. 13:2). Several Scriptures
describe the fierceness of a bear with cubs (cf. 2 Sam. 17:8; Prov. 17:12; Hosea 13:8).

This refers to the Medo-Persian Empire (cf. Dan. 8:21). Possibly the "raised on one side"
may refer to

- the supremacy of Persia (see note at Dan. 5:28)

- preparing to attack again, even though it was still eating the last victim (imagery for
unsatiated power and military destruction)

▣ "three ribs" The NRSV and NAB translate this Aramaic term as "tusks" (Hebrew BDB 854,
Aramaic form BDB 1106). This probably comes from the basic meaning of the Hebrew counterpart, taken from
the Arabic "curved." But also other usages of the Hebrew root are a play on the word "side" (i.e. rib
of a hill, side chambers, rib of a tree or plank, BDB 854).

The controversy over the etymology of this term is related to its use in Gen. 2:21-22.
The New International Dictionary of OT Theology and Exegesis, vol. 3, p. 811, gives an alternate
possibility of the term "rib," as being confused with the Sumerian term for "life." How this would affect
this verse in Daniel is uncertain.

This is a parallel to the ram of Dan. 8:4, where the ribs may relate to the three
directions or areas of conquest: Babylon to the West, Lydia to the North, and Egypt to the South. Ben Ezra
thinks they refer to three cities which were conquered. We know from historical records that Medo-Persia
did not have many conquests to the East until the reign of Darius I Hystaspes.

of the ancient Fertile Crescent.

7:6 "a leopard which had on its back four wings of a bird" This refers to the speed of the military
conquest of Alexander the Great. Greece then is the third predatory Gentile Empire (cf. Dan. 8:21). The
symbolic number "four" may refer to its conquest of the whole known world (cf. Dan.7:2). See chart in Contextual
Insights to Daniel 8.

▣ "also had four heads" This specific detail about the number of Alexander's generals who
succeed him, has caused many modern scholars to reject the predictive nature of Daniel. Yet, the affirmation
of a supernatural God revealing to a faithful servant for the purpose of affirming His sovereignty to later
generations seems perfectly adequate to explain this detailed description of history.

All of these details are not prophetic. Commentators must look to history to help interpret
ambiguous apocalyptic passages. The four heads may refer to (1) extensive conquests in all directions or
(2)four regional generals of Alexander the Great. Alexander died from a fever at the young age of 32
while in Babylon (or some say Egypt). His kingdom was initially divided among five generals, but four
of them became dominant:

- Ptolemy in Egypt

- Cassender in Macedonia and Greece

- Seleucus in Syria and Babylon

- Lysimichus in Thrace

Antigonus ruled part of Asia Minor for a brief period, but was killed in 301 B.C.
and was only of minor influence and importance.

7:7 "a fourth beast" By the sequencing of chapters 2, 7, and 8 of Daniel (see Textual Insights A.,
B., and C.) this refers to the Roman Empire. This would correlate with the iron and clay legs and feet
of Dan. 2:33,41-43.

The fourth empire is characterized in several ways.

- dreadful, Dan. 7:7,19

- terrifying, Dan. 7:7

- extremely strong, Dan. 7:7

- iron teeth, Dan. 7:7,19 (dual in Hebrew, possibly two large teeth or two rows of teeth)

- devoured, Dan. 7:7,19

- crushed, Dan. 7:7,19

- trampled down the remainder with its feet, Dan. 7:7,19

- ten horns, Dan. 7:7,20

- a boastful little horn, Dan. 7:8,20

- claws of bronze, Dan. 7:19

Several of these terms are used in different senses in the book, which shows how context
determines meaning.

- "dreadful" is used of

- the image in Dan. 2:31 and translated "awesome"

- Daniel's fears in Dan. 4:5 and the people's fear in 5:19

- "devour" is used

- literally in Dan. 4:33; 7:5,7,19

- as imagery for slander in Dan. 3:8; 6:25

- "crushed" ("broke in pieces") is used literally in Dan. 7:7,19,23

- also literally of the Messiah breaking the image in Dan.2:35,45

- also literally of the lions crushing those who falsely accused Daniel in 6:24

▣ "ten horns" This may speak of ten simultaneous kings (cf. Dan. 2:44). Because three of
them are ripped out at the same time (cf. Dan. 7:8,24), they must be simultaneous. However, I believe
them to be symbols of completeness or of power (cf. Zech. 1:18-21; Rev. 13:1), not literal kings which
commentators try to fit into known history.

The term "horns" (BDB 1111) often stands for "kings" (Daniel 7 & 8) or "power"
(OT imagery, i.e., the horns of the sacrificial altar and altar of incense).

- the Anti-Christ of the end-time because it comes from the fourth kingdom (Futurism, cf. H. C. Leupold,

This is somewhat confusing because the "little
horn" of Dan. 8:9-14 seems to refer to the Seleucid ruler, Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164

These "little horns" are both arrogant and boastful. They reject the worship of YHWH
and try to destroy His people. They are both allowed by God to prosper and both will be destroyed by
